passage: I'm Arnab. When Kalyani presented her project on rivers, she twirled the end of her plait round her finger, tugged her sleeve and straightened her collar twice. Behind me, someone whispered, “She doesn't know it, look at her hair.” I didn't agree. She answered every question the teacher asked, clearly and correctly. I think she was just nervous, since she looks like that every time she stands in front of the class. Afterwards I said, “Nice presentation.” She grinned and let go of her plait.

qa.q: What did Kalyani twirl round her finger?
qa.a: She twirled the end of her plait round her finger.

qa.q: What was Kalyani probably feeling, and what shows that the fidgeting was not proof of not knowing?
qa.a: Probably mild nervousness, since she does it every time she stands in front of the class. She answered every question clearly and correctly, so the twirling did not mean she did not know.

qa.q: What could someone do instead of whispering guesses about her hair?
qa.a: Notice what she actually says and, afterwards, offer a kind word, as Arnab did.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel about the whisper, "She doesn't know it"?
qa.a: Arnab may have felt it was unfair, since Kalyani answered every question clearly and correctly, and Arnab praised her afterwards.

grounding: Twirling hair and tugging clothing are self-comfort acts showing mild tension, not lying.

passage:
Monday: in the class quiz, Pema twirled her hair round her finger before each answer. Varun thought, She doesn't know the answers.
Wednesday: Varun stood to read his poem. His hands went to his collar and tugged it straight, and then his sleeve. He noticed, and thought, That's what nerves do to me.
Friday: Pema twirled her hair again at the quiz. This time Varun did not guess anything. He gave her a small thumbs-up. She smiled, and gave the right answer.

qa.q: What did Pema do with her hair before each answer on Monday?
qa.a: She twirled her hair round her finger before each answer.

qa.q: What did Varun think on Monday about Pema's twirling, and what changed his view?
qa.a: He thought she did not know the answers. After noticing his own nervous tugging on Wednesday, he saw the twirling was probably nerves too, and on Friday he felt sympathetic enough to give her a thumbs-up.

qa.q: What small step did Varun take on Friday?
qa.a: He gave Pema a small thumbs-up and did not guess anything, which was kind and gave her some support.

qa.q: How might Pema feel when Varun gives her a thumbs-up?
qa.a: Probably reassured, since she smiled and gave the right answer. She may not have known he noticed.

grounding: Hair twirling and clothing adjusting are self-comfort acts under mild tension, not signs of not knowing.

passage: Hemant, you tug your collar just like I used to twirl my hair. Let your Lalremsiami Pi, your grandmother, tell you. When I was eleven, in Aizawl, I was picked for the school quiz final. On stage I twisted a lock of hair round and round my finger and kept pulling my sleeves over my hands. An aunty in the front row whispered, loud enough, “Look at her, playing with her hair for the boys' team.” My face burned. I wasn't looking at anyone; I was terrified of the buzzer. Afterwards my mother took that aunty aside, and she said, “She fiddles when she's nervous. Nothing more.” We came second. I still twirl my hair on planes.

qa.q: Where was the school quiz final?
qa.a: The quiz final was in Aizawl.

qa.q: What was young Lalremsiami feeling as she twisted her hair on stage?
qa.a: She was terrified of the buzzer, and twisting her hair and pulling her sleeves helped her cope with the nerves.

qa.q: What choice did her mother make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She took the aunty aside and explained it was nerves, which corrected the unfair reading without shaming anyone in public.

qa.q: How did the aunty in the front row read the hair-twirling?
qa.a: The aunty read it as flirting with the boys' team, missing that it was a nervous habit.

grounding: Shows a child twirling hair and tugging sleeves from nerves, and why observers should not read it as flirting.

passage: With five minutes before the bell, Vasudha Ma'am called Ankita to the front to ask about the missing library book. Ankita stood straightening her tie, tugging her sleeves down over her wrists, tugging again. Two boys at the back whispered, “She's lying, look at her fidgeting.” Vasudha Ma'am heard. She knew Ankita did this before every speech and every test. “Ankita, I'm not accusing you. I just need to know when you last saw it.” Ankita's hands stopped for a second. “Friday. I put it on the return shelf.” Vasudha Ma'am turned to the class. “Fiddling with clothes means nerves, not lying. Let's check.” The book was there, behind the atlases.

qa.q: Where did Ankita say she put the book?
qa.a: She put it on the return shelf.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as she tugged her sleeves?
qa.a: Ankita was nervous about being questioned in front of the class, as she is before every speech and test.

qa.q: How did Vasudha Ma'am handle the whispers?
qa.a: She reassured Ankita she wasn't accusing her, told the class that fiddling with clothes means nerves, not lying, and then checked the shelf.

qa.q: How did the boys at the back read Ankita's fidgeting?
qa.a: They read it as a sign of lying, which was unfair since it only showed nerves.

grounding: Shows a child tugging sleeves and straightening a uniform when nervous, and an adult teaching that it is not a sign of lying.

passage: At the society meeting in their Mumbai building, Raghav stood up to present his idea for a Sunday clean-up. He kept pushing up his glasses, straightening his collar, tugging at the hem of his T-shirt. One uncle muttered, “Why so fidgety? Must be his father's idea, not his.” Raghav heard and tugged his collar harder. Nirmala Aunty, the secretary, raised her hand. “Take your time, Raghav. I fiddled with my dupatta at every meeting for ten years.” A few people laughed kindly. Raghav let go of his collar, took a breath and explained his plan, with a chart he had drawn himself. The vote was yes.

qa.q: What did Raghav propose?
qa.a: Raghav proposed a Sunday clean-up.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as he tugged his collar harder?
qa.a: Raghav was nervous about speaking to the adults and stung by the uncle's remark, so he fiddled more.

qa.q: How did Nirmala Aunty help Raghav?
qa.a: She gave him time and shared her own fiddling habit, which eased his tension so he could explain his plan.

qa.q: How did the uncle read Raghav's fidgeting?
qa.a: The uncle took it as a sign the idea wasn't really Raghav's, misreading nervous fidgeting as dishonesty.

grounding: Shows a child adjusting clothing and glasses from nerves, and an adult showing it only means mild tension, not dishonesty.

passage:
"Your turn, Zubin. Tell us about your trip to Ladakh."
"Um. Okay." Zubin tugged his sleeve down over his wrist. "We saw a lake that was three different blues."
He straightened his collar. Then his tie. Then his collar again.
"He's making it up," muttered Karan. "Look at him fiddling."
"He's not," Rafiq whispered back. "He does that every time he has to talk in front of people. He did it at his own birthday."
"…And a yak walked right past our tent." Zubin tugged the other sleeve.
Karan snorted. "A yak?"
"There are yaks in Ladakh, Karan," said Ms Iyer. "Go on, Zubin. Did it notice you?"
Zubin's hands dropped to his sides. "It sniffed my shoe."

qa.q: What did Zubin say the lake looked like?
qa.a: A lake that was three different blues.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling as he tugged his sleeves and kept straightening his collar?
qa.a: Nervous and self-conscious about speaking in front of the class; the tugging comforted him and says nothing about whether his story is true.

qa.q: How did Ms Iyer help Zubin relax?
qa.a: She backed up his fact about yaks and asked a friendly question, so his hands dropped to his sides.

qa.q: How did Rafiq see the fiddling, compared with Karan?
qa.a: Rafiq knew it was Zubin's usual nervous habit, while Karan wrongly took it as a sign of making things up.

grounding: It shows a child tugging sleeves and straightening his collar from nerves while speaking, which a classmate wrongly reads as lying.
